By Gavin van Marle
18 November 2026
MSC’s East Mediterranean transhipment hub, in the Turkish port of Tekirdag, is set to almost triple the handling capacity at its Asyaport facility.
There are plans to expand the Asyaport terminal, which is 75% owned by MSC, and 25% by the local Soyuer Group, and increase capacity from the current 2.75m teu to 4m teu by the end of the year.
The terminal’s deepsea berths are being extended from 1km to 1.4km, while an adjacent feeder pier has already been extended, to 710 metres.
The fresh capacity is needed by both port and carrier – according to Xeneta’s eeSea liner database, Asyaport handled 2.2m teu last year, representing an annual utilisation rate of 78%, pushing the facility into territory where outbreaks of congestion can be difficult to clear.
Throughput this year hit 1.86m teu in the first 10 months, which analysts at Alphaliner suggested “the port is on course to exceed last year’s record”.
They noted: “The Turkish port exclusively handles MSC vessels and operates its own towage and pilotage services. Transhipment accounts for 80% of its throughput, leaving 10% each for exports and imports from and into Turkey via the European side of the Marmara Sea.”
According to eeSea, MSC has some 14 feeder and intra-Europe services calling at the terminal, using it as its gateway to the Black Sea, as well as its Asia-Europe Tiger service, operated in conjunction with Premier Alliance members, and transatlantic EMUSA service.
Meanwhile, according to Alphaliner, a third and fourth expansion phase have already been developed by the terminal, with planning approvals in place, that would ultimately take Asyaport’s capacity up to 6m teu a year, and cement its place as the largest container facility in the country.
Image: Alphaliner
“A third expansion phase, for which the necessary permits are prepared, would sacrifice a 310-metre feeder berth for land reclamation, increasing the container yard area with another 30,000 sq metres,” Alphaliner writes.
“The fourth phase would see the length of both the deepwater and feeder pier extended by 700 metres, bringing the total quay length to 2,810 metres.
“Timing will depend on future cargo demand at Tekirdag,” the analyst added.

BRUSSELS — The European Commission on Wednesday proposed a new €45 billion ($49.5 billion) loan to Ukraine to help fill a funding gap of €70 billion for next year as Kyiv continues its fight against Russia’s 2022 invasion.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Ukraine would only need to repay the loan after Russia had paid reparations for damage caused by the war.
The planned measure, which requires approval from EU member countries, would come on top of a similar loan of €90 billion to Ukraine agreed by EU leaders at the end of last year to fund Ukraine in 2026 and 2027.
“Five years since the start of this war of aggression, Europe stands united,” von der Leyen told reporters in Brussels. “We are as committed as ever to support Ukraine in war and in peace.”
Kyiv’s other international partners would be expected to provide the rest of the money to fill next year’s funding gap, von der Leyen said.
The Commission, the executive body of the 27-nation European Union, proposed that to up to €25 billion from the new loan could be spent on military aid and up to €20 billion on general budget support.
To finance the loan, the European Commission would borrow on behalf of the EU on international markets, officials said.
Intensified Russian attacks
European Economy Commissioner Valdis Dombrovskis said Ukraine needed additional support because Russia is intensifying attacks on critical infrastructure and disrupting trade, particularly by blocking Black Sea export routes.
“For almost five years, Ukraine has stood guard against the Russian aggression that also threatens our citizens, our territory, and our way of life. Our support gives Ukraine a crucial strategic partner,” he said.
Von der Leyen said she was confident all EU members would back the new loan, even though three – Hungary, the Czech Republic and Slovakia – opted out of the last one.
She said even EU countries that did not favor giving military aid to Ukraine were still committed to supporting Kyiv more generally, so their support for the loan could be attributed to meeting civilian needs.

The Chinese biotech will work with Pfizer on three in vivo CAR T therapies for autoimmune indications.
Pfizer is officially entering in vivo CAR T with China’s RNA-focused biotech Starna Therapeutics in a deal that could reach $2.6 billion.
The new partners will work together to develop three CAR Ts for automimmune disease that are currently preclinical. Pfizer has offered $330 million upfront plus up to $2.3 billion in milestones as well as royalties.
While Pfizer has previously examined ex vivo CAR T in oncology, this deal marks the first time the Big Pharma has worked on in vivo CAR T, a spokesperson confirmed to BioSpace Wednesday morning. The deal will bolster Pfizer’s immunology and inflammation (I&I) pipeline.
“B-cell depletion therapies have been an area of interest for Pfizer, and we are particularly excited to research and advance therapies designed to generate CAR-T cells inside the body,” the spokesperson said.
Pfizer has also secured the rights to use Starna’s in vivo CAR T technology for I&I and oncology indications, according to the spokesperson. A separate research collaboration could also yield future compounds, although details were not disclosed.
Starna is developing RNA medicines delivered via a targeted lipid nanoparticle (LNP) platform. Pfizer, meanwhile, has significant scientific expertise in RNA delivery, the spokesperson added.
“Combined with Starna’s programs and technology, those capabilities give us a powerful way to pursue this next-generation approach in cell therapy,” they said.
China has been a frequent source of deals for Pfizer. The New York pharma inked a massive 10-asset deal with Innovent in May that could ultimately pay out $10.5 billion.
The company is also working with Sciwind Biosciences to market an obesity treatment in the country. That deal was signed in February , with Pfizer paying $495 million upfront.
At the same time, Pfizer CEO Albert Bourla has expressed concern about the rise of China and the need for Big Pharmas like his to find ways to cut costs with AI to match the nation’s prowess at accelerating drug development.
Pfizer is jumping into the CAR T space at a time when peers like Novartis and Bristol Myers Squibb are responding to safety concerns about the use of these complex therapies in more common autoimmune conditions. Both Novartis and BMS have paused ongoing clinical trials amid reported safety events, including deaths.

Posted By: Henry Lazenby November 18, 2026
TDG Gold (TSXV: TDG; US-OTC: TDGGF) has drawn up a plan to mine two gold and silver deposits in northern British Columbia, days after agreeing to sell a majority stake in a nearby property to Freeport-McMoRan (NYSE: FCX). The first preliminary economic assessment (PEA) for Shasta and Mets puts the upfront cost of two open pits and a shared mill at $605 million (US$423 million). The deposits, in the Toodoggone district about 430 km northwest of Prince George, would produce 71,200 oz. of payable gold and 2.82 million oz. of payable silver a year over 9.9 years. “The PEA defines what we can evaluate economically today,” Paul Geddes, TDG’s senior vice-president of business development and strategy, said Tuesday in a release . “It does not define the limits of a mineralized district.” TDG would keep both deposits and collect $110 million in cash if the Aurora West sale closes. For an explorer that put its cash at about $2 million when it announced the deal, that would pay for more drilling and engineering at Shasta. Building the mine would take considerably more capital. TDG shares slipped 2.7% to close at 72¢ in Toronto on Tuesday, valuing the company at about $200 million.
One mill
Silver would account for 36% of gross metal revenue over the life of the operation at the study’s prices of $50 per oz. silver and $3,550 per oz. gold, both in U.S. dollars. TDG estimates an after-tax net present value of $1.18 billion, using a 5% discount rate, and an internal rate of return of 39%. Cutting both prices by a fifth brings the estimated value down to $703 million and the return to 27%. Shasta would feed a 4-million-tonne-a-year mill, with higher-grade material from Mets added in years four and five. The plan includes inferred resources that would need further drilling and study before they could be considered for a reserve. The Nov. 17 resource estimate gives Shasta indicated resources of 17.12 million tonnes at 0.87 g/t gold and 31.73 g/t silver, containing 479,000 oz. of gold and 17.46 million oz. of silver. Inferred resources total 26.84 million tonnes at 0.47 g/t gold and 20.57 g/t silver, for 406,000 oz. of gold and 17.75 million oz. of silver. Higher metal-price assumptions helped bring more low-grade material into the modelled pit. Mets’ first estimate shows inferred resources of 530,000 tonnes at 2.47 g/t gold and 0.1 g/t silver, containing 42,000 oz. of gold and about 2,000 oz. of silver.
Noncore sale
The Freeport deal still needs TSX Venture Exchange approval. Freeport has committed to spend at least $30 million on exploration in the three years after closing. That counts towards the $80 million in exploration spending required to raise its stake in the main joint venture to 75%. Exercising the option would also require Freeport to pay TDG another $40 million in cash for full ownership of two separate claims. TDG would retain a 2% net smelter return royalty on those claims. At Shasta, TDG expects the proposed development to need both a provincial environmental assessment certificate and a federal impact assessment decision. One issue for regulators is Jock Creek, which the mine plan would divert in year four. That would require separate authorization under the federal Fisheries Act.

By Alex Lennane
18 November 2026
EU imports of low-value ecommerce goods fell 63% year on year in the quarter immediately after the bloc introduced its €3 customs duty in July.
Now, with an added €2 handling fee in force since 1 November, Seko Logistics is warning UK retailers that some Black Friday bundles could incur €15 in customs charges – before VAT.
The EC’s preliminary assessment counted 555 million low-value ecommerce items entering the EU in Q3, down from 1.51 billion a year earlier, and said some goods appeared to be coming in as bulk shipments for storage and fulfilment within the bloc. The figures cover the period before the 1 November fee.
This year’s Black Friday, on 27 November, will be the first since the EU removed its duty exemption for low-value parcels. Where both charges apply, each distinct line on the customs declaration adds €5. A jumper, candle, and mug declared on three lines would incur €9 in duty and €6 in handling fees, before VAT is added.
“The retailers that will feel it most are the ones whose best-selling deals are bundles,” said Steve Aylott, Seko’s UK and Ireland sales director.
“Five euros per product type sounds small, until it is sitting on a £20 Black Friday deal,” he added. “Retailers have to decide whether to absorb it, build it into European prices, or rethink the bundle. What they can’t afford is a customer finding out after they’ve paid.”
The origin of the goods can also change the bill. Goods that qualify for UK ‘preferential treatment’ can avoid the €3 duty if they are entered on a full customs declaration and VAT was collected outside the EU’s Import One-Stop Shop. The €2 handling fee still applies, and is non-refundable if the goods are returned.
“Where a parcel ships from and where the goods come from are two different questions,” said Tim Harding, Seko’s UK and Ireland customs manager. “Customs looks at origin and classification. If the product data behind a Black Friday order is wrong, the duty will be wrong too, and peak is the worst possible time to find out.”
Air cargo gateways are already seeing a change in the mix. Liège Airport said small-parcel volumes fell 42% after the July duty took effect, reducing the number of dedicated ecommerce flights. Total Q3 cargo tonnage was virtually flat year on year, at 334,467 tonnes.
WorldACD said Hong Kong-Europe air cargo chargeable weight, across all commodities, was still down 32% year on year in the week of 2–8 November.
At TIACA’s Air Cargo Forum in Miami in October, Rotate’s Ryan Keyrouse identified Liège and Budapest as European ecommerce gateways hit by falling demand. Across the affected Europe-bound traffic, other commodities had not replaced the lost ecommerce volumes as they had following changes to US de minimis rules, he said.
“You see that no other commodity picked up to backfill that,” he said. Airlines had, instead, redirected capacity from Europe towards North America and intra-Asia markets.
For retailers with steady EU demand, Seko said holding stock inside the bloc could make sense, allowing them to import in bulk and fulfil orders locally. Shein, which opened its Wrocław logistics hub in December 2025, said this month it was investing €500m this year to expand the operation.
Meanwhile, the decline could spread further: the UK government plans to scrap customs duty relief on imports worth £135 or less by October 2028, six months earlier than originally planned.
Goods will become subject to standard UK tariff rates, and the government plans a separate fee to cover the cost of processing low-value imports. Ministers have yet to set the fee, or decide whether to charge it per parcel or per item. A House of Lords subcommittee took evidence on the reforms last week and is due to hear from Treasury minister James Murray and HMRC officials tomorrow.
Elsewhere, J&T Express reported a record 136m parcels across its global network on 12 November, the day after China’s Double 11 shopping event. It averaged 119m parcels a day from 1 to 12 November, up 26% year on year.

SONAR’s new Sitrep, The Lag Effect, shows rates rising far faster than costs, capacity leaving at a record pace, and contract rates with more room to run in 2027.
Truckload rates have finally outrun the cost of running a truck. SONAR’s spot linehaul index (NTIL) is up about 49% in a year and dry van contract base rates (VCRPM1) about 25%, while industry non-fuel operating costs rose 4.2%. Yet more than 1,000 logistics job cuts and 15 bankruptcy filings landed in just a few weeks this fall.
Both things are true at once, and the reason matters for every shipper heading into 2027 bids. SONAR’s new Sitrep, The Lag Effect, breaks down the data.
Are truckload rates higher than carrier costs now?
Yes. Spot linehaul (NTIL.USA) is $2.60 a mile, about $0.75 above ATRI’s 2025 industry non-fuel cost of $1.854. That reverses three straight years, from 2023 through 2025, in which spot linehaul ran below carriers’ non-fuel costs.
Spot linehaul (NTIL): $2.60 a mile, up about 49% year over year.
Contract base rate (VCRPM1): $2.88 a mile, up about 25%.
Diesel ( DTS ): $6.15 a gallon, up about 62%, adding roughly $0.36 a mile in fuel cost.
Non-fuel operating cost (ATRI): up 4.2% in 2025, to a record $1.854 a mile.
SONAR National Truckload Index, Linehaul Only (NTIL.USA), five years | Current: $2.60 | 5-yr Avg: $1.95
If rates are up, why are carriers still going bankrupt?
Because the recovery arrived after three years of erosion. In 2022, dry van contract linehaul cleared carriers’ non-fuel costs by about $1.01 per loaded mile. By 2025, that cushion was down to about $0.26. Many small, spot-dependent carriers burned through their cash before rates turned.
Fuel makes it worse for the smallest operators. Spot rates are quoted all-in, with no separate fuel surcharge, so a load-board carrier absorbs every diesel spike until the market reprices. Larger fleets on contract freight recover most of it. The bankruptcies in the headlines are the bill for 2023 through 2025, not a sign the market is still falling.
How fast is trucking capacity leaving?
Faster than SONAR has ever recorded. The count of tractors in for-hire fleets (TCFH.USA) is 1,551,161, down about 107,000 from a year ago, including about 51,000 in a single month this summer. It is the largest decline in a series that runs back to 2008.
Tender rejections confirm the squeeze. The SONAR Truckload Rejection Index ( STRI.USA ) is 12.87%, about double a year ago and more than three times its October 2023 level, while truckload volume (STVI.USA) is roughly where it was in October 2023. Fewer trucks are competing for about the same freight.
Some of the fleet-count drop may reflect FMCSA’s new Motus registration system, which launched in May. But public carriers’ own earnings point the same way: Knight-Swift’s average tractors fell 4% and Schneider’s 8% year over year, and Schneider’s and Werner’s one-way fleets are down a combined 38% since 2021.
SONAR Tractors from Fleets Authorized for Hire (TCFH.USA), 2008 to present | Current: 1,551,161
Where is the truckload market tightest?
The national average hides a split market. The Northwest (23.19%) and Midwest (17.55%) are rejecting far more tenders than the national rate of 12.87%, while most of the biggest Sun Belt markets are loose.
Tightest markets: Quincy, Ill. (49.42%), Pendleton, Ore. (42.18%), Spokane (39.34%) and Sioux Falls (38.21%).
Largest markets, still loose: Atlanta (7.82%), Dallas (7.91%) and Houston (6.49%).
By equipment: reefer (STRIR) and flatbed (STRIF) rejections are both above 21%, and spot rates for van, reefer and flatbed are each up roughly 50%.
SONAR Truckload Rejection Index by region, Oct. 2023 to present | Northwest 23.19% | Midwest 17.55% | National 12.87%
What should shippers expect in 2027 contract bids?
More increases. Dry van contract base rates are still about 6.5% short of the level that covers carrier overhead, and the spot-contract gap has halved in a year, from about $0.57 to $0.28 a mile. Reefer has the most catching up to do: reefer contract base rates (RCRPMF) are up only about 8% and now sit about $0.30 a mile below dry van contract.
The Sitrep’s base case calls for dry van contract increases of about 5% to 8%, with double-digit increases if capacity keeps leaving. Shippers should price routing guides lane by lane rather than off the national index.
What’s inside the full Sitrep
The carrier cost stack, line by line, and what the 2026 diesel spike did to cost per mile
For-hire and fleet-size tractor counts, including how capacity is moving from owner-operators to mid-size fleets
Five years of fleet data from Knight-Swift, Schneider and Werner, split by one-way and dedicated
Regional and market-level rejections for all 135 SONAR markets
Van, reefer, flatbed and intermodal signals, and three 2027 contract rate scenarios
All SONAR Sitreps and the data behind them are available in the SONAR platform. Request a demo . Sitreps are also available with a subscription to FreightWaves Market Monitor at getfreightdata.com .
Frequently asked questions
Why are trucking companies going bankrupt in 2026?
Most failing carriers spent 2023 through 2025 hauling at rates below their costs and ran out of cash before 2026’s rate recovery reached them. Small, spot-dependent carriers were hit hardest because they get no fuel surcharge and pay more per truck for insurance.
How much have truckload rates risen?
SONAR’s spot linehaul index (NTIL) is up about 49% year over year to $2.60 a mile, and dry van contract base rates (VCRPM1) are up about 25% to $2.88 a mile, as of Nov. 13, 2026.
Is trucking capacity shrinking?
Yes. SONAR’s count of for-hire tractors (TCFH) is down about 107,000 year over year, the largest decline in its history back to 2008. Tender rejections (STRI) have doubled to 12.87% on volume roughly flat with late 2023.
Will truckload contract rates rise in 2027?
The data points that way. Contract rates are still about 6.5% short of covering carrier overhead, and the gap between spot and contract has halved in a year. Reefer contract rates, up only about 8%, have the most room to rise.
What is a tender rejection rate?
It is the share of contracted loads that carriers turn down. SONAR’s Truckload Rejection Index (STRI) tracks it daily; a rising rate means carriers have better options than their contracted freight .
Sources: SONAR (NTIL, NTI, VCRPM1, RCRPMF, DTS, TCFH, STRI, STRIR, STRIF, regional STRI, STVI), pulled Nov. 13, 2026; ATRI, Analysis of the Operational Costs of Trucking: 2026 Update (July 2026); Knight-Swift, Schneider and Werner earnings releases and SEC filings; layoff and bankruptcy counts compiled by FreightWaves.

By: Northern Miner Staff November 18, 2026
Agnico Eagle Mines (TSX, NYSE: AEM) heads into its capital markets day Wednesday with a goal of producing more than 4 million oz. of gold a year in the early 2030s and a nearer-term test in Quebec, where it must bring more underground ore to surface as mining winds down in the Canadian Malartic pit complex. The company expects this year’s production near the bottom of its 3.3-million to 3.5-million-oz. range after ground movement forced it to revise the mining plan at the Barnat pit. Agnico has identified 2030 as the first year of a bigger increase in group output. Its investor webcast is scheduled for 10:30 a.m. Toronto time. “Most of our peers will do 30 or 40% detailed engineering before they announce a project,” CEO Ammar Al-Joundi said at a Toronto symposium on Nov. 9. Agnico is prepared to spend more on engineering before committing to construction to reduce the risk of cost overruns, he said.
Underground push
At Canadian Malartic, the question is how quickly underground development can replace lost open-pit tonnes and fill the mill. The Barnat ground movement could cost Agnico up to 150,000 oz. in each of 2027 and 2028, the company said in its third-quarter results.
The Odyssey underground operation mined a record 391,000 tonnes in the third quarter. East Gouldie, one of its deposits, produced 27,250 oz. Agnico has said further investments could help bring Canadian Malartic’s annual production towards 1 million oz. as early as 2033. Nunavut’s Hope Bay provides a measure of what the next ounces could cost. Agnico approved the project in May at an estimated initial cost of $2.4 billion (C$3.4 billion). Production could begin as early as 2030 and average 435,000 oz. a year once the operation reaches a steady rate, the company said in its investment decision. Agnico shares closed C$3.20 stronger at C$247.49 in Toronto on Tuesday. They have traded between C$188.48 and C$348.94 over the past year.

The Army has acknowledged the difficulty. In Breaking Defense’s October 15 reporting , Liz Miranda, Army Materiel Command’s executive deputy to the commanding general, said the White House directive to map supply chains down to the raw-material level “is no easy task.”
For magnet buyers, that challenge combines sourcing, manufacturing, and qualifications into the same conversation. A supplier must demonstrate the required magnetic properties, support delivery commitments, and provide the necessary proof of the material pathway behind its products.
Evolution Metals & Technologies, known as EM&T, is addressing that challenge through its established magnet manufacturing operations in South Korea, additional feedstock commitments, and an expansion now underway. The company has also announced plans to develop U.S. manufacturing and critical materials recovery capabilities, including recycling end-of-life magnets to recover materials for new production and support supply chains aligned with applicable U.S. sourcing requirements.
The Sourcing Challenge Reaches Beyond the Factory
Beginning January 1, 2027, the Defense Federal Acquisition Regulation Supplement (DFARS) 252.225-7052 expands restrictions for covered contract deliveries to include materials mined, refined, separated, melted or produced in China, Russia, North Korea or Iran.
Specialized manufacturing equipment. Image Courtesy of Evolution Metals & Technologies
For neodymium-iron-boron magnets, the restriction extends from mining neodymium, iron and boron through finished magnet production. Samarium-cobalt magnets face expanded supply-chain restrictions as well, subject to applicable exceptions.
EM&T Builds its Material Supply Position
EM&T already manufactures and sells bonded and sintered magnets. Its October 28 and 29 announcements describe eight customer-certified high-performance sintered magnet grades, providing an established product foundation for its expansion.
On October 29, 2026, EM&T repo r ted securing approximately 754 metric tons of neodymium metal sourced outside China , approximately 42 metric tons delivered to Pohang, 72 metric tons pending shipment through March 2027 and 640 metric tons committed through the end of 2027 . The committed portion includes a 600-metric-ton Senri Trading contract.
Experienced operators at work. Image Courtesy of Evolution Metals & Technologies
For procurement teams, those categories make the supply position clear. Received inventory supports near-term production planning; committed volumes give visibility into supply through 2027.
EM&T has sourced some materials from China for its broader commercial business. For defense applications, the company intends to supply magnets that meet the expanded requirements through a documented sourcing pathway, with origin and processing history tied to each production lot.

David Wilcox, Executive Chairman of the Board of Evolution Metals & Technologies (NASDAQ: EMAT). Image Courtesy of Evolution Metals & Technologies

“We already produce N42SH commercially, a grade the Army identifies as acceptable for its small-drone motor requirement. Our capability statement proposes a staged qualification process supported by auditable mine-to-magnet traceability for each production lot. Our focus is demonstrating how our manufacturing capabilities and sourcing documentation can meet the customer’s specific requirements.”

Ben Collins (left) and Johan Beal (right) Photo: Alison Koo
By Alison Koo
18 November 2026
Demand for project cargo across Asia is expected to surge in the near term, but the industry’s capacity to transport such shipments is struggling to keep pace with the rapid development of projects.
At Breakbulk Asia in Singapore today, MSC’s head of project cargo, Ben Collins, said the region was becoming increasingly important to the successful execution of major infrastructure and industrial projects.
“Vietnam has an emerging nuclear power programme; Asia is very central to the supply and successful delivery of these projects, so it’s time for optimism and bullishness.”
AAL Shipping’s commercial chief, Felix Schoeller, explained that geopolitical developments had accelerated the relocation and expansion of engineering, procurement, and construction (EPC) activities in Asia.
“There has been a big push in the last 10 years, going back to the first Trump administration, which resulted in the China Plus One strategy, boosting manufacturing capacity across South-east Asia and India,” he said.
However, some executives warned that inadequate landside infrastructure and logistical constraints could hamper the movement of oversize and heavy cargo.
Kohki Uemura, CEO of Japanese heavylift forwarder Denzai, identified road and bridge infrastructure as a major bottleneck when transporting modules weighing between 500 and 1,500 tonnes, adding: “Roads and bridges are not enough for such heavy cargo.”
Yohan Beal, Ceva Logistics’ operations director for Asia Pacific, said responsibility for addressing these challenges rested with the parties conducting logistics surveys and overseeing project requirements.
“Is due diligence being done?” he asked. “Can I make sure that I can actually get the cargo out of the port? Can I actually deliver the cargo from the port to the final destination?
“Those are the parameters we need to ascertain before we actually fix the port of discharge and the final route we take,” he added.
Mr Beal noted that project owners and EPC contractors were increasingly recognising the importance of incorporating logistics considerations at an early stage, leading them to involve specialist logistics providers earlier in the planning process.
“Since the pandemic, people who used to be underappreciated in the logistics field are now making their way to the boardrooms. Clients now seek approval before purchase orders are signed,” he said.
Mr Collins echoed the call for earlier planning, cautioning project owners against prioritising short-term cost savings at the expense of future transportation requirements.
“Don’t be dictated by looking for a cheaper price tomorrow… what you might have to move today is going to cost you more tomorrow,” he said.

Pfizer CEO Albert Bourla is no longer looking around at his immediate peers for the next competitive threat. He’s eyeing an entire nation poised to take over the global biopharma business.

Summit Therapeutics was warned twice by the FDA that the Phase 3 trial used to support the application for ivonescimab did not include patients that accurately represented the American population.
In rejecting Summit Therapeutics’ PD-1xVEGF the FDA raised concern about the high rate of Chinese patients included in the final dataset, as well as potential safety concerns with the addition of VEGF inhibition.
The FDA on Tuesday afternoon published the Complete Response Letter that rejected Summit’s ivonescimab. The overall rejection was based on the fact that Summit’s application did not provide substantial evidence of effectiveness or establish a positive benefit-risk profile for ivonescimab’s use in EGFR-mutated non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC).
Summit, which announced the rejection on Sunday morning, had submitted the application based on an improvement in progression-free survival (PFS), but the Phase 3 trial did not show an overall survival (OS) benefit in this population. A post-hoc analysis was submitted in September to support OS.
But the agency was not convinced—and reviewers’ concerns seem to go deeper than just the PFS endpoint.
Safety, Chinese population questioned
In the letter, agency staff explained that efficacy in a U.S. population could not be established because 93% of the events that showed progression-free survival occurred in patients that had been enrolled in China. During meetings in March 2023 and again in May 2025, the FDA warned that this would be a problem, according to the letter.
This Phase 3 study was originally designed as a single-country trial in China but was modified to include North American and European patients—but that didn’t occur until May 2023, according to the letter. As a result, the trial population remained heavily skewed toward Asia, and the applicability of progression-free survival could not be determined for U.S. patients.
On the PFS endpoint, the FDA agreed that this endpoint was statistically significant but the effect size was “modest” in the context of an add-on to chemotherapy. The drug also did not show improvement of OS or overall response rate.
Summit submitted a post-hoc analysis in an attempt to bolster the application this fall—at the 11th hour. The FDA was not swayed. While this data package included longer follow-up, the reviewers dismissed it as exploratory only. Moreover, the data cutoff dates (DCO) were different across the regions presented.
“These differential DCO dates appear to be due to termination of follow-up at an earlier date for patients enrolled in China compared to patients enrolled in NA and EU, with clinical sites in China closing during 2025,” the letter states.
Finally, on safety, the FDA raised concerns about the modest PFS improvement given the added risk of serious immune-related toxicities and toxicities known to VEGF inhibition. The letter does not go into detail about the possible safety risk.
For Summit to rectify the issues, FDA reviewers recommended a new, adequate and controlled multi-regional clinical trial of ivonescimab in EGFR-mutated NSCLC. This trial must show statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvement in OS, PFS or another endpoint that measures clinical benefit to gain approval, the reviewers added. They also suggested, however, that Summit meet with the FDA before proceeding with such a trial.
Summit licensed ivonescimab from China’s Akeso, which has already secured approval there for this indication and several others. Summit’s challenge was to reproduce the promising data seen in Chinese patients that had analysts dubbing the drug a potential “Keytruda killer”—referring to Merck’s mega-blockbuster immunotherapy cancer drug, which ivonescimab bested in a head-to-head trial in the Asian country.
The rejection has raised concerns across the entire PD-1xVEGF class , which includes candidates from Bristol Myers Squibb and BioNTech, plus Pfizer, Merck and AbbVie.

Now, for example, FreightSuite and Shipthis are pitching themselves as CargoWise replacements, GoFreight is courting similar customers, and Magaya has named two forwarders that chose its software over CargoWise.
Magaya even points to the moves on its website, saying: “CargoWise, built by WiseTech Global, has long dominated the highest enterprise tier of freight forwarding software. Magaya was built for a different kind of company: small to mid-market freight forwarders and customs brokers who run integrated warehouse operations, value responsive support, and need software they can actually go live on without a six-month project and a dedicated consultant.
“That distinction has always existed, but recent events at WiseTech Global have brought it into sharp focus, prompting forwarders across the industry to take a hard look at what they’re paying, what they’re getting, and what alternatives look like.”
But how far do those alternatives extend for forwarders that need one system across multiple countries?
That question has reached the European Commission. In August, a submission seen by The Loadstar asked the EC to monitor whether CargoWise’s reach and WiseTech’s acquisitions could make it harder for forwarders to switch, or for rival vendors to connect to customs systems on equal terms. The submission alleged no breach of competition law. The commission said it had put the information on file.
In Australia, the competition regulator took action in a separate case. The ACCC accepted a court-enforceable undertaking from WiseTech and its subsidiary, BluJay, to divest Expedient, a logistics software business acquired through e2open. The regulator said WiseTech already had substantial market power and that bringing CargoWise and Expedient under the same ownership reduced choice for Australian customers. WiseTech and BluJay disputed that assessment.
Rivals acknowledge how hard it is to compete for the largest accounts. “There is really no alternative to CargoWise for the biggest global forwarders,” Benjamin Riege of Germany’s Riege Software told The Loadstar in February. “But when you’re a medium-sized forwarder, of course we are a choice.”
For a multinational, switching means getting the new software to work with the customs authorities, carriers, and customers its branches already deal with. Can staff file declarations from the new platform in every country in which they need to? Can the finance teams keep invoicing while open jobs and unbilled charges are moved across? Will staff still be able to retrieve the records they need for an audit?
AI may help vendors build customs integrations faster, one freight software executive told The Loadstar , but “the actual government sign-off is always going to be the bottleneck”. The same executive sees a reason for AI vendors to take on the core platform itself. “The system of record is going to be what owns the AI and the process, going forward,” he said.
Rivals can point to some wins. Magaya said in January that EP Logistics had selected its software to replace CargoWise across its US and Mexican operations. In May, it announced that Montreal-based CMS Shipping had also chosen to switch. WiseTech, meanwhile, said it had secured CargoWise rollouts with 13 of the world’s 25 largest forwarders as of 30 June, and named Blue Water Shipping and XPD Global among the contracts won under its new pricing model.
The next CargoWise renewal may be where forwarders first feel the benefit of more competition. A credible alternative gives them more room to negotiate on price and support, even if they ultimately decide to stay.

Layoffs at the FDA, disruptions to research funding and increased tariffs led the investment banking firm Cassel Salpeter to wonder whether the government is strangling the biotech industry.
Tariff uncertainties, FDA drama and other government actions in the U.S. are deterring investors from backing early-stage biotechs and adding to existing funding challenges, according to investment bank Cassel Salpeter.
The argument that the U.S. government may be hurting the industry centers on the Trump administration’s approach to the FDA, research funding, onshoring and tariffs , according to the firm’s new third-quarter healthcare investment report.
“The ongoing uncertainty of the impact of tariffs is keeping investors on the sidelines when it comes to early-stage companies,” the Cassel Salpeter report read. “Combined with the slowdown of federal grants and an increase in operating costs, the current environment makes the fundraising task extremely difficult.”
Some of the actions have hurt small biotechs more than large drugmakers, Cassel Salpeter added. Smaller companies may lack the resources to onshore manufacturing, exposing them to tariffs that larger drugmakers have avoided by committing to U.S. investments and striking deals with the government. Larger companies may also be better positioned to absorb the cost of any tariffs they do need to pay.
Cassel Salpeter identified other ways in which tariffs disproportionately affect small- to mid-sized biotech companies, noting that the levies increase the cost of imported materials needed for the lab work that is central to research-stage startups.

While Congress has pushed back against the funding cuts, the investment bank noted “major disruptions” in the funding of new applications and renewals of existing grants and contracts. The Trump administration has also taken actions that have affected drug developers of all sizes, Cassel Salpeter noted. The report outlines the layoffs , delays and upheavals that shook the FDA after Trump began his second term in January 2025.
The investment bank shared its analysis of the government’s impact on biotech alongside data on M&A and private placements. LIMiK Capital, LLC is setting up a manufacturing facility in Cherokee County, South Carolina, to build heavy-duty power transformers. The $327.7 million investment will create 400 new jobs , Gov. Henry McMaster’s office announced.
What’s Related
The plant will sit in Meadow Creek Industrial Park at 34 Commerce Drive in Gaffney, on the former TTI property. The company expects operations to be online in early 2028.
LIMiK Capital is a subsidiary of LIMiK International LLC, an American maker of large power transformers. LIMiK International has 25 years of experience designing and building power transformers, autotransformers, and generator step-up units for utilities, independent power producers, contractors, and defense facilities across the country. The company said every unit is custom-engineered and built in the U.S. to meet the grid conditions of the industry it serves.
What the plant will build
The Gaffney site will handle the full build from start to finish. That includes core cutting and stacking, coil winding, drying and oil processing, tank and enclosure work, final assembly, and factory acceptance testing before units ship .
“At a time of rising costs and growing demand for electricity, this plant, built on the former TTI property, will supply utilities, manufacturers and businesses across the Southeast and the United States with the transformers they need,” said Igor Lon, managing director and co-owner of LIMiK International.
Lon added, “We share that confidence in Cherokee County’s workforce and its future, and we look forward to becoming part of the South Carolina economy as a long-term employer and a good corporate citizen of this community.”
State and local leaders react
McMaster tied the project to rising power needs.
“As demand for reliable energy continues to increase, investments like this will help strengthen our nation’s power infrastructure while creating new opportunities for South Carolinians,” he said.
Secretary of Commerce Harry M. Lightsey III said, “LIMiK Capital’s $327.7 million investment in Cherokee County will propel our state’s economy forward.”
Cherokee County Council Chairman Tim Spencer said the project gives new life to an existing industrial site.
“Transforming the former TTI property at 34 Commerce into a state-of-the-art power transformer manufacturing plant marks another significant milestone in the continued growth and diversification of our industrial base,” Spencer said. “This is exactly the type of investment that moves Cherokee County forward.”
The Coordinating Council for Economic Development approved job development credits for the project.

If you wake up tomorrow as the esteemed Lord Mayor of London, you’ll want to make a properly dignified entrance. To make sure your arrival turns the right heads, Electrogenic has taken the Mayor’s 1973 Roll-Royce Phantom VI and turned it into a properly traditional standard-bearer with modern electric power.
The stately, stylish, and silent electric Rolls-Royce car made its public debut at last month’s Salon Privé weekend at Blenheim Palace, where it joined a growing fleet of classic Rollers that have received Elctrogenic’s electric conversion, including the stunning Mulliner-bodied 1929 Phantom II that we covered back in 2023 .
For this project, Electrogenic carefully removed the internal combustion-based engine, transmission, and fuel system from the City of London Corporation’s official ’73 Phantom VI limo and replaced it with a 120 kW (~160 hp) electric motor putting out 310 Nm (~230 lb-ft) of torque. Sharp-eyed readers will note those numbers are significantly lower than what you’d expect from the 6.2L L410 V8 fitted with twin SU carburetors (as it was in the standard ’73 IV), but since those numbers were never officially published, we would say that the power available from the new electric drivetrain is similarly adequate for Mayoral use.
Power for the electric motor comes from a 62 kWh li-ion battery fitted under the hood bonnet, and offers more than enough range to get the Lord Mayor to their appointments in and around the city.

Keeping it classy
Under the bonnet; by Electrogenic.
To ensure the heads of the heads of the city don’t bob in an undignified manner while on parade, Electrogenic added a “ceremonial” drive mode that trims power and torque and softens the throttle map, so the chauffeur can more easily hold the crawling pace demanded by civic processions and state occasions.
“We were honored to be asked to electrify this significant motor car, and to play a part in the City of London Corporation’s journey to net zero,” says Steve Drummond, chief executive of Electrogenic. “When it was launched in the late 1960s, the Rolls-Royce VI was the most refined and dignified limousine on the road. Now, thanks to electrification, its core character has been enhanced further: it is whisper quiet, effortless to drive with swift performance, and emits zero tailpipe emissions.”
Only Phantom VIs were built, with this 3 meter-long coach-built limousine having been commissioned during the mayoralty of Alderwoman Dame Susan Langley DBE, the 697th Lord Mayor of the City of London. Over the weekend, the FDA rejected Summit Therapeutic’s Akeso-partnered ivonescimab. Had the decision gone a different way, it would have been the first PD-1/VEGF bispecific to hit the U.S. market, but because the Phase 3 HARMONi trial failed to show an improvement in overall survival, the FDA decided that Summit had not provided enough evidence of the drug’s efficacy in patients with EGFR-mutated non-small cell lung cancer to support an approval.
Other drugmakers advancing assets in this up-and-coming drug class —including BioNTech and partner Bristol Myers Squibb, plus Pfizer, Merck and AbbVie—are now all on notice of the bar they will need to pass to win an FDA nod.
The Summit decision was one of the most closely watched on the FDA’s docket this month , but still to come are decisions on Capricor Therapeutics’ Duchenne muscular dystrophy cell therapy, which was already rejected once and suffered a negative adcomm meeting this fall, and Vertex Pharmaceuticals’ investigational IgA nephropathy medicine—an approval for which could push the big biotech into its next era .
Outside of the FDA, the biggest news of the week came from Isomorphic Labs, which on Tuesday announced a $5 billion series C fundraise —the largest in the industry’s history. The news follows closely on the heels of the AI drug discovery biotech’s $2.1 billion series B in May, meaning the company has raised at least $7.7 billion to date without entering the clinic—or even declaring a pipeline.
Also this week, two big conferences— ObesityWeek and Clinical Trials on Alzheimer’s Disease (CTAD)—have spawned a ton of headlines.
At Obesity Week, Novo’s next-gen obesity candidate CagriSema, which is currently under FDA review with a decision expected by the end of the year, showed comparable results at lower dose levels as it had at the higher dose levels, for which results were first announced back in late 2024. Wave Life Sciences, meanwhile, presented the first data from the highest dose cohort of its GalNAc-siRNA weight loss candidate, WVE-007, showing that higher baseline body mass index and excessive body fat have been associated with a more pronounced effect. And at CTAD, drugmakers showcased novel modalities, such as AriBio’s PDE5-inhibiting drug, which slowed cognitive decline in patients with Alzheimer’s disease when used as a monotherapy, hitting one of the dual primary endpoints in the Phase 3 trial.
Finally, former FDA Commissioner Marty Makary’s Commissioner’s National Priority Voucher program may finally be winding down , according to media reports. This news came days before the Senate prepares to vote on Heidi Overton as the next permanent FDA commissioner.
And check out BioSpace ’s latest dispatch on women in the industry , with a recent Bedford Group report showing that while women have made gains in boardrooms, rising to 29% representation in 2025’s fiscal year, that hasn’t translated to more female CEOs.

By Charlotte Goldstone
18 November 2026
Transatlantic airfreight rates have hit their highest level since December 2022, as peak-season demand and tightening capacity push prices up – although last week’s US aviation disruption appears to have had little additional impact.
According to Freightos, Europe-US rates jumped 12% last week, to $3.27 per kg, while China–North America prices rose 16%, to $9.25 per kg, already exceeding last year’s December peak of $8.
The increases predated the nationwide US flight grounding on 13 November, neither lane recording a significant further rise following the disruption.
Thomas Cullen, Transport Intelligence analyst, noted that the FAA failure appeared to have had “remarkably little impact” on US airfreight operations. UPS and FedEx had warned of possible delays, while Delta briefly embargoed pharmaceutical and fresh cargo, lifting the restrictions the following day.
Meanwhile, data supplied to The Loadstar by freight forwarder ExFreight suggested transatlantic increases had accelerated sharply this month.
For shipments of more than 100kg, the average Europe-US rates remained virtually unchanged between June and October, at around $3.06 per kg, but jumped 25%, to $3.83, this month. Asia-US rates rose more moderately, increasing 10% between June and November, from $7.81 to $8.63 per kg.
However, individual European lanes recorded considerably steeper increases. Denmark–US rates soared 191%, from $2.55 to $7.41 per kg, while Sweden prices rose 59%, France 53%, Austria 47%, Switzerland 39%, and the UK 25%.
In Asia, South Korea prices recorded a 64% increase, followed by Indonesia, at 53%, Hong Kong 34%, Japan 28%, China 21%, and Malaysia 14%.
Conversely, rates from India fell 17%, Sri Lanka 14%, and Taiwan 7%, highlighting the uneven nature of the market.
Charles Marrale, CEO of ExFreight, told The Loadstar : “Honestly the market is very weird right now. We are seeing larger accounts slow down, but then we are adding on a lot of new business from smaller accounts.”
He said the company’s API connectivity was attracting smaller businesses embracing AI and looking to integrate freight providers directly into their enterprise resource planning systems.
Meanwhile, Cathay Cargo reported an 8% year-on-year increase in October tonnage, despite available freight tonne km rising just 1%. Tonnage for the first 10 months was up 9%.
The carrier attributed the growth primarily to strong exports from North-east and South-east Asia, with network equipment shipments supporting demand for Cathay Priority and semiconductor traffic underpinning Cathay Expert.
It said it expected demand to remain strong through the traditional peak season and plans to introduce an additional A330 freighter, operated by Air Hong Kong, on selected regional routes.
Freightos suggested Europe-US demand was being supported by seasonal volumes and Asia-origin cargo seeking alternative routings, while reduced winter passenger schedules and freighter redeployment could be further restricting capacity.
Mr Marrale warned that reductions in US airline capacity, driven by higher fuel costs and weaker passenger demand, could keep prices elevated.
He also highlighted the continuing Middle East tensions, noting passenger demand to Dubai remained 28.1% below last year’s levels, with the wider region down around 30%.
“I don’t expect Gulf capacity to increase until the current situation with Iran is settled,” he said.
Looking ahead, Mr Marrale suggested potential US tariff reductions under the incoming Congress could prompt importers to rush to restock, triggering another increase in airfreight rates.
However, he acknowledged that the absence of a veto-proof majority made any legislative changes uncertain.

Thanksgiving can leave loaded trailers sitting for days while terminals close and fewer employees are around to watch them. Before the break, carriers should figure out where freight will be parked and how it will be protected.
What’s Related
J. J. Keller ’s Josh Lovan, a former undercover detective and carrier safety director, is urging carriers to secure freight before the holiday. His white paper, Cargo Security and Preventing Theft in Trucking , outlines steps they can take.
1. Plan where freight will sit
Start with parking. Keller recommends well-lit spots with controlled access, fencing, and cameras, and says to avoid leaving loaded trailers unattended whenever possible.
The white paper calls for locking loaded inbound and outbound trailers during closed hours. It also lists four ways to secure loaded trailers during closures or whenever they are unattended: padlocked, docked, butted or blocked.
For security-sensitive freight, back swing-door trailers against a dock and overhead-door trailers against another trailer. Keller recommends both padlocks and kingpin locks for these loads.
Door locks restrict access to cargo , while kingpin locks help prevent unauthorized hookup to a tractor. Straight trucks and pickup-and- delivery trailers should have their cargo compartments locked away from the terminal except during loading and unloading.
RELATED STORIES: Fake Pickups Top the Worry List as Cargo Theft Gets More Organized | Half of Cargo Theft Cases Now Linked to Trusted Carriers
2. Check the yard and keep watch
Before closing, check gates, lighting, cameras, and alarms. The paper lists high-definition cameras that retain at least 60 days of footage among its suggested security measures.
Drivers leaving a truck unattended at a closed terminal should shut off the engine, close the windows, and lock the doors. The key should go with the manifest in the terminal’s designated spot.
GPS tracking and tamper alerts can flag unexpected movement or interference with a shipment . Carriers should also set driver and dispatcher check-in procedures and make clear how to report suspicious activity.
3. Inspect loads and document problems
Drivers should verify loads before leaving and check seals at every stop. The paper recommends documenting high-value goods with photos, serial numbers, and other identifying details that could help establish what went missing.
Only the designated supervisor should have access to the seal supply, and a distribution log should be maintained. Before accepting trailers from a railroad yard or another carrier, drivers should check seal integrity, record the seal number, and report discrepancies immediately.
“There is no single lock, camera or piece of technology that will prevent every cargo theft,” Lovan said.

“We are hiring drivers at a pace that’s equivalent to where we were at the peak of Covid,” CFO Brad Delco told investors at the Stephens Annual Investment Conference in Nashville, Tennessee.
J.B. Hunt ( NASDAQ: JBHT ) incurred costs from adding several driver-hiring associates at the end of the summer, alongside an undisclosed number of new drivers. While these onboarding efforts generated temporary cost and productivity headwinds, the new recruiting team has reached target performance levels. Ongoing technology investments are enabling the company to fulfill driver demand during the current upcycle with a 30% smaller staff.
Delco said some cost buckets are up by mid-single- to low-double digits, and that these increases will have to be recouped through pricing in order to restore margins and justify capacity additions. Surging fuel costs have resulted in a 100-basis-point margin headwind this year, but volatility on that cost line has calmed in recent weeks. However, elevated group medical costs continue to be a headwind across all industries.
The company has removed $135 million in annual costs (about 1%) over the past year, and reminded investors that cost management is “a continuous event.” J.B. Hunt’s earnings turnaround started in the 2025 third quarter.
Equipment costs, Montgomery ruling push dedicated demand to new high
J.B. Hunt’s dedicated pipeline remains at an all-time high even as it continues to convert prospects into new accounts at an accelerated pace. The company sold service on 425 trucks in the third quarter (970 trucks year-to-date), putting it on pace to exceed its annual target for net truck additions of 800 to 1,000.
The company’s dedicated sales team focuses on converting private fleets into J.B. Hunt assets.
Many businesses are no longer willing to fund non-core capex (tractors and trailers) as equipment costs have increased. Also, the Supreme Court’s broker-liability ruling has shippers rethinking liability risk, with the group becoming more willing to outsource the driver-vetting function to an operator like J.B. Hunt. Further, driver recruiting in an upcycle is difficult for private fleets, which don’t carry specialized hiring teams.
Startup costs from the recent account wins, however, will likely be a modest drag on margins in the near term. Dedicated contracts are typically structured as five-year deals, with breakeven results taking approximately six months to achieve.
BNSF temporary outage produces minimal Q4 volume headwind
Management also quantified the impact from flooding along BNSF’s (Berkshire Hathaway, NYSE: BRK-B ) Southern Transcon line. It said the heavy rains resulted in a three-day outage, impacting approximately 7,500 loads. That represents roughly 1% of J.B. Hunt’s 550,000 quarterly intermodal shipments. There were no material cost impacts from the event.
SONAR: Intermodal Contract Savings Index (IMCSI.USA). The IMCSI shows the savings percentage between domestic intermodal contract rate per mile and truckload contract rate per mile. The comparison includes fuel surcharges.
The company’s intermodal bid season begins in October each year. It said intermodal is currently 30% to 35% cheaper than truckload. Inflections in TL pricing typically lead changes in intermodal pricing by six to nine months, placing J.B. Hunt in an advantageous position as truck pricing has been on the rise for nearly a year.
It said last week at a separate investor conference that the market will likely be supportive of inflation-plus pricing. However, it doesn’t expect intermodal to fully close the pricing gap to truck as TL rates continue to reset higher.
The company reprices 10% of its intermodal book in the fourth quarter and 30% in each of the remaining three quarters.
Shares of JBHT were down 3.4% in Tuesday trading compared to the S&P 500, which was off 1%.
Why it matters? Driven by heightened regulatory enforcement and the Supreme Court’s broker-liability ruling, shippers are increasingly outsourcing trucking functions to dedicated fleets.

A new factory near Raleigh, North Carolina, will assemble and test electrical equipment before it ships to data centers and other project sites. Siemens said on Tuesday that it opened the 131,000-square-foot plant last week and expects it to create up to 200 skilled manufacturing jobs .
What’s Related
The factory builds power skids, which combine pieces of electrical equipment on a single platform. Siemens assembles, connects, and tests the equipment at the plant before shipping it as a unit. That leaves less work for crews at the construction site and can help data center operators bring new capacity online sooner.
Part of a $165 million-plus expansion
Siemens first announced the Raleigh-area factory in March as part of a plan to invest more than $165 million in manufacturing across North and South Carolina. At the time, the company expected the Raleigh-area site to add 100 jobs by the end of 2026. Its opening announcement put the total at up to 200 jobs and gave no hiring timeline for the full tally.
The March plan also included expanding switchgear production in Wendell, North Carolina, and building a new lighting panel plant and distribution center in Spartanburg, South Carolina. Siemens said the investments would help it fill record orders for electrical equipment used in data centers.
Siemens is working with Wake Technical Community College to train new hires. The college’s onboarding program, Operation Boot Camp, teaches basic mechanical and electrical skills used in manufacturing.

source_document.body:
Redwood Logistics is telling shippers to slow down any 4PL selection that shows one of nine warning signs, starting with managed transportation rebranded as a 4PL. The checklist anchors the State of 4PL 2027 report the Chicago-based company released Nov. 11, a 43-page case for what it calls an open 4PL.
The report arrives nearly a year after Gartner’s first Magic Quadrant for fourth-party logistics named Redwood a Visionary , as shippers struggle to get a return on technology they already own. Redwood argues fragmented provider networks are the reason, and that AI makes the problem more expensive.
Redwood frames the fix as a choice about who adapts to whom.
“Every 4PL relationship embeds a fundamental architectural choice: either the provider adapts to the shipper’s ecosystem, or the shipper is forced to adapt to the provider’s closed stack,” said Mike Reed, Redwood’s chief product officer, in the release.
That gap shows up in PwC’s 2026 Digital Trends in Operations Survey of 767 U.S. operations and supply chain leaders, where 89% gave at least one reason their tech investments haven’t fully delivered the expected results, with integration complexity at the top of the list. The 2025 edition put the figure at 92%, the number Redwood cites in its release.
Nine warning signs for 4PL buyers
The list covers managed transportation rebranded as 4PL, visibility without resolution, closed technology or provider requirements, savings guarantees based primarily on procurement, undefined AI claims, heavy dependence on manual coordination, no dedicated continuous-engineering resources or measurable improvement backlog, ambiguous decision rights, and no credible benefit-measurement methodology.
The report adds two tests adapted from Better Supply Chains’ 4PL NExus checklist. First, shippers should ask what share of a provider’s exceptions are resolved by system-executed actions and how many hours pass between a disruption and the provider’s executed fix.
“A provider that cannot answer is describing visibility, not execution,” the report says.
Second, shippers should check whether their current provider is paid on a cost-plus, transactional basis or shares financial risk through an outcome-based agreement.
“The most useful questions a shipper can ask an orchestration partner are the ones a provider cannot answer with a slide,” said Erin Breen, Redwood’s chief growth officer, in the release.
What separates a 4PL from a 3PL
Gartner defines a 4PL as a provider that engages in “the design, build, implementation and ongoing orchestration” of all or part of a logistics network, according to the report. A 3PL runs a defined function such as transportation, warehousing, or customs. A 4PL governs the providers and systems around it.
Redwood splits that category in two. In what it calls a closed 4PL, the shipper standardizes on the provider’s TMS, a fixed carrier set, and a bundled service scope. In an open 4PL, the provider connects to the systems the shipper already runs and picks carriers and tools for each job, including ones that compete with its own offerings. Redwood moved to its modern 4PL positioning after Gartner analysts rejected the company’s original platform label .
Redwood’s five-level maturity model
The report’s five-level maturity model runs from fragmented logistics through managed execution, a connected control tower, and continuous orchestration to an adaptive supply chain. Redwood places most North American shippers at Level 2 or Level 3.
The climb to Level 4 is the steepest, according to the report, because three things have to be true: the provider holds authority to act, the network runs a closed loop from sensing a problem to learning from the fix, and engineering becomes a standing function. The report also says a focused midmarket shipper can operate at Level 2 for years. At Level 1, it says, agentic AI automates the fragmentation.
“Deploying advanced technology or agentic AI into a fragmented network simply automates the chaos,” said Eric Rempel, Redwood’s chief innovation officer, in the release. “Our research found that only 13% of shippers deploying AI see quantifiable results, because unintegrated data and fragmented tools act as instant innovation blockers.”
That figure comes from Redwood’s AI in Logisti cs report , released in May and drawn from the company’s Customer Advisory Board. The May report described the figure as applying to companies actively deploying AI. Redwood did not disclose how many companies responded. Rempel warned at a FreightWaves event in July that supply chain AI is nearing the Trough of Disillusionment .
Switching costs and RedwoodConnect
Integration debt keeps shippers with providers past the point where the relationship works, the report says, because carrier relationships, system integrations, data history, and team workflows all tangle with the incumbent.
Redwood’s answer is RedwoodConnect, an integration platform the company says links to more than 150 products and platforms. In a typical engagement, it connects 3.5 systems per client, with 85% of connections running over API, 10% over EDI, and 5% still manual. The company added Cincinnati-based managed transportation provider Stridas in March, a week after buying Laredo, Texas, customs broker EELCO, and is connecting Stridas to that platform.
The report cites TileBar, a tile and bath design company with nine showrooms, as one result. Redwood kept many of its incumbent carriers, added two experienced in residential freight, and remapped its LTL pool distribution network, including new pool points for an expansion into Arizona. The report puts the combined procurement and optimization savings at more than $2 million.
The trade-offs in an open model
But the report concedes the model’s cost. Openness “swaps the shipper’s lock-in risk for a heavier governance and integration burden on the provider,” it says. It also says none of Redwood’s design choices is unique to the company in principle. And the Level 2 or 3 placement is Redwood’s own assessment, which the report does not tie to survey data.
Among its 10 predictions through 2031, the report says neutrality will become a leading criterion in 4PL selection, with neutrality and portability clauses in contracts as the early indicator.
“Optionality given up in year one is extraordinarily expensive to buy back in year four,” Breen said.
Why it matters: Shippers narrowing their roster of logistics providers can use the report’s tests to check a 4PL’s execution and exit terms before signing, when leaving costs the least. The signal to watch is whether neutrality and portability clauses start showing up in new 4PL contracts.

U.S. shippers can now take a photo of an item and use it to draft a customs description when booking an international shipment with DHL Express. The company launched the AI tool in the U.S. this week ahead of the holiday shipping season .
What’s Related
The tool suggests a description within seconds. Customers can accept, edit, or replace it before submitting the shipment. They can use a smartphone or another connected device, and a DHL Express account is optional.
How it works
The feature is built into DHL Express’s international booking process. It uses computer vision, a type of AI that identifies objects in images, to recognize the item in a photo and draft a description for customs paperwork. DHL said the launch marks the first time this kind of tool has been built into a live booking process at scale.
DHL says inaccurate or incomplete descriptions are a common reason shipments get held up at customs. The tool is meant to help customers get the description right while they’re still preparing a shipment, with the goal of improving data quality and reducing the potential for delays.
When DHL first announced the tool in May, Dirk Olufs, the company’s global chief information officer, said accurate item classification at the point of data entry “means cleaner data across the entire shipment lifecycle.” Neither DHL announcement gave figures on how often the tool identifies items correctly or whether it has reduced customs holds in markets where it’s already available.
RELATED STORIES: Why Customs Expertise Gives North American Supply Chains an Advantage | Ranking the World’s 25 Largest Air Freight Forwarders
The importance of small and midsize businesses
Small and midsize businesses account for about 86% of DHL Express’s U.S. customers. The number of U.S. businesses in that group using DHL Express to send exports rose 6% year over year, the company said.
DHL says smaller companies often have fewer resources to handle customs paperwork than larger companies with dedicated trade compliance staff.
“For many businesses, one of the most challenging parts of international shipping is simply describing what they are sending to meet regulatory requirements,” said Greg Hewitt, CEO of DHL Express U.S. “With AI-powered item identification, we’re taking the guesswork out of that process.”
Enna Zarate, DHL Express senior vice president of digital customer solutions, said in May that the feature “is a direct response to customer feedback.”
Where the tool is available
DHL first announced the tool on May 7, when it was live in eight markets, including Germany and Singapore. The U.S. is now one of 10 markets in the Americas where customers can use it, alongside Brazil, Canada , Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Ecuador, Guatemala, Mexico and Peru.
The May announcement called for more launches through 2026. With the U.S. launch, DHL said it expects the rollout to continue into 2027.

Posted By: Henry Lazenby November 18, 2026
Koryx Copper (TSXV: KRY; NSX: KYX; US-OTC: KRYXF) is proposing a bigger mine at its Haib project in Namibia, where a new study raises the upfront cost by 32% and planned annual payable copper output by 41% for the first decade.
The first prefeasibility study (PFS) puts the cost of building Haib at $2.06 billion (C$2.94 billion), up from $1.56 billion in the September 2025 assessment. The open pit would yield 130,000 tonnes of payable copper a year over its first decade, up from 92,000 tonnes. Haib is about 780 km by road south of Windhoek, near the South African border.
A simpler plant and less waste rock to move make the study “a clear de-risking step,” Red Cloud Securities mining analyst Ian Parkinson wrote Wednesday. “In our view, a stressed Orange River remains the main risk,” he added.
First reserve
The study gives Koryx its first mineral reserve at Haib and a mine plan to take to potential partners. Koryx estimated its cash at C$35 million at the end of October in an investor presentation. It is seeking financing while it prepares a definitive feasibility study.
“The PFS cements our view that Haib is a buildable large-scale project,” Haywood Securities mining analyst Jamie Spratt wrote Tuesday, citing its infrastructure and location. “We expect this will make the full suite of strategic options available to management” as it pursues financing and permits, he added.
Koryx shares fell 7.8% to C$3.18 at Tuesday’s close in Toronto, valuing the company at about C$390 million. Spratt kept his buy rating and C$8 target. Parkinson kept his buy rating and raised his target to C$6.50 from C$5. Red Cloud disclosed it had provided investment banking services to Koryx in the past year.
The upfront cost exceeded BMO Capital Markets mining analyst Rene Cartier’s $1.7-billion estimate. But stronger-than-expected production in the early years would help Koryx recover its investment sooner, he wrote Tuesday. Life-of-project cash costs of $2.19 per lb. also came in below his $2.66 estimate. Cartier raised his target to C$6.50.
Higher grades first
At a copper price of $5 per lb., Haib has an after-tax net present value of $2.54 billion at an 8% discount rate, and a 25% internal rate of return, Koryx said. The September 2025 assessment put the value at $1.35 billion and the return at 20%, based on $4.31 per pound.
The revised plan would move 0.98 tonne of waste per tonne of ore over the life of the project, down from 1.88 tonnes in the earlier study. Koryx also dropped heap leaching. Its redesigned plant would discard about a quarter of the crushed rock before final flotation. The mine would send higher-grade material to the mill first and save lower-grade rock for the final nine years, when the plant would run on stockpiles. Over 24 years, Haib would average 105,000 tonnes of payable copper, 12,000 oz. of payable gold and 1.13 million lb. of payable molybdenum a year.
The Nov. 6 estimate puts Haib’s probable reserve at 1.12 billion tonnes at 0.27% copper, 58 parts per million molybdenum and 0.02 g/t gold. The reserve contains about 3 million tonnes of copper, 65,000 tonnes of molybdenum and 689,000 oz. of gold.
Permitting
Koryx applied for a mining licence in September 2025 and submitted its mine environmental assessment in August 2026. The project would need about 20 million cubic metres of water a year. Koryx plans to draw from the Orange River only when flows exceed the needs of downstream users and the environment, and store the surplus behind an off-channel dam. The study budgets $80 million for the water supply works and $26 million for the dam.
The operation would use grid power supplemented by on-site solar and battery storage. Koryx aims to secure major permits around mid-2027 while it works on a definitive feasibility study. CEO Heye Daun is targeting early works late next year and construction in the first quarter of 2028.

The FDA has granted accelerated approval to GSK’s tyrosine kinase inhibitor neladalkib for ALK-positive non-small cell lung cancer, marking the second regulatory win from the pharma’s $10.6 billion takeover of Nuvalent Bio earlier this year.
The approval, which came 10 days ahead of the Nov. 27 target action date, allows the use of neladalkib for patients with advanced disease who have undergone prior lines of treatment for unresectable tumors. To keep the approval, GSK will need to confirm the drug’s clinical benefit in a confirmatory study. Neladalkib will be marketed under the brand name Nelkarmi, according to a Tuesday announcement .
GSK acquired Nuvalent in June for $10.6 billion in one of the industry’s largest buys this year. The main bounties from the takeover were the biotech’s two lead non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) assets: the ROS1 inhibitor zidesamtinib, which the FDA approved in July as Jideytro, and Nelkarmi.
Aside from Jideytro and Nelkarmi, Nuvalent also brought GSK the HER2 blocker NVL-330, which is in Phase 1 development for NSCLC.

Nelkarmi’s approval was supported by data from the Phase 1/2 ALKOVE-1 study, which enrolled 700 patients with ALK-positive solid tumors, GSK said on Tuesday . One of the trial’s primary outcomes is objective response rate (ORR). Nelkarmi resulted in a 49% ORR in patients whose only prior exposure to ALK-targeted tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) was through Genentech’s Alecensa. In patients who had received at least two prior lines of ALK TKI therapy, ORR was 32%.
Nelkarmi was designed to address drug resistance and treat NSCLC that has spread to the brain, GSK said in the Tuesday release. In ALKOVE-1, intracranial ORR hit 55% in patients with measurable metastasis in the central nervous system and whose only prior ALK TKI was Alecensa.
Nelkarmi had previously bagged the FDA’s breakthrough therapy designation, which is granted to therapies that address a serious disease and have shown early evidence of substantially improving outcomes versus available therapies.
As for tolerability, GSK noted that 5% of treated patients had to permanently discontinue Nelkarmi due to adverse reactions, the most common of which was liver toxicities. The drug’s prescribing information carries warnings and precautions for hepatotoxicity, renal toxicity, ocular toxicity, creatine phosphokinase elevation and embryo-fetal toxicity. Other common side effects include constipation, muscle or bone pain, edema and fatigue.
GSK is running the Phase 3 ALKAZAR study for Nelkarmi in TKI-naive ALK-positive NSCLC patients and other solid tumors.
